questions.q: Describe the three movements of ocean water.
answer: Ocean water is never still; it moves in three main ways — waves, tides and currents.

answer.text: Waves are caused by winds blowing over the surface of the sea. Strong waves erode the coast, while a tsunami is a giant wave caused not by wind but by an undersea earthquake or volcano.
Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea water, usually twice a day, caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun.
Currents are streams of water flowing continuously in a definite direction — warm currents from the equator towards the poles and cold currents from the poles towards the equator.

answer: These movements shape coasts, climate and marine life.

questions.q: Explain spring and neap tides, and why the meeting of warm and cold currents is important.

answer.text: When the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line, at full moon and new moon, their combined pull produces the highest tides, called spring tides.
When the Sun and Moon are at right angles to the Earth, at the first and last quarter of the Moon, their pulls partly cancel out, giving the lowest tides, called neap tides.

Where a warm current, such as the Gulf Stream, meets a cold current, such as the Labrador Current, the mixing of waters supports abundant plankton and fish, creating some of the world's richest fishing grounds, though it also causes dense fog.
